etymology: From craft, skill — and the drift of the English word from skill to cunning is itself the moral history the Bible describes.
biblical_def: Crafty is skill bent to deceive. Job states the doctrine that keeps the crafty from being feared: God “taketh the wise in their own craftiness” (Job 5:13), a line Paul quotes to the Corinthians to deflate their admiration of clever men (1Co 3:19). Paul refuses the method for himself — “we have renounced the hidden things of dishonesty, not walking in craftiness, nor handling the word of God deceitfully” (2Co 4:2) — and warns that the serpent beguiled Eve “through his subtilty” (2Co 11:3).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines crafty as cunning, artful, skilful in devising and pursuing a scheme, by the use of stratagem or deception.
webster_full: CRAFTY, a. Cunning; artful; skilful in devising and pursuing a scheme, by the use of stratagem or deception.
2. Artful; cunning; in a good sense, or at least without blame.
scriptures: Job 5:13
He taketh the wise in their own craftiness: and the counsel of the froward is carried headlong.
For the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God. For it is written, He taketh the wise in their own craftiness.

But have renounced the hidden things of dishonesty, not walking in craftiness, nor handling the word of God deceitfully; but by manifestation of the truth commending ourselves to every man's conscience in the sight of God.
But I fear, lest by any means, as the serpent beguiled Eve through his subtilty, so your minds should be corrupted from the simplicity that is in Christ.
corruption_summary: Craft is now a marketable competence — messaging, spin, optics — and the church has imported the whole toolkit under the banner of communicating effectively.
corruption_paragraphs: Paul's renunciation in 2 Corinthians 4:2 is remarkable for what it gives up. He forswears not merely lying but craftiness — the arts of framing, timing, and selective emphasis by which a true statement is made to serve a false impression. His alternative is stated in the same breath: by manifestation of the truth commending ourselves to every man's conscience in the sight of God. The gospel is to be set out plainly and left to do its own work on the conscience.

Job 5:13 supplies the reason the crafty are never finally impressive: God taketh the wise in their own craftiness. The scheme is the trap. Haman built a gallows, Absalom hired a counsellor, the Sanhedrin arranged a sealed tomb — and in each case the machinery of cleverness became the instrument of reversal. A believer confronted with sophisticated opposition may take considerable comfort in the pattern.
roots_summary: Hebrew arum (H6175), subtle, shrewd — used of the serpent in Genesis 3:1; Greek panourgos (G3835), ready for anything, unscrupulous.
roots_lines: Hebrew arum (H6175) — subtle, crafty; the serpent was more subtil than any beast of the field (Gen 3:1).
Greek panourgia (G3834) — craftiness; 1 Corinthians 3:19, 2 Corinthians 4:2 and 11:3.
Greek dolioo (G1387) — to use deceit; Romans 3:13, with their tongues they have used deceit.
usage: “He taketh the wise in their own craftiness” — the scheme becomes the snare.
“Not walking in craftiness, nor handling the word of God deceitfully” — the apostolic renunciation.
“The serpent beguiled Eve through his subtilty” — craft's first success.

etymology: The KJV spelling of subtle, from Latin subtilis, finely woven. Subtlety is a fine weave — a thing whose seams cannot be seen.
biblical_def: Subtil describes cunning so fine it is undetectable. It is the Bible's first adjective for the enemy: “Now the serpent was more subtil than any beast of the field which the LORD God had made” (Gen 3:1), and the subtlety consists in a question rather than a claim — yea, hath God said? Jonadab is called “a very subtil man” and uses the gift to engineer Amnon's crime (2Sa 13:3). Proverbs however can use the same root approvingly, of prudence that foresees evil (Pro 22:3), which is why Christ commands serpent-wisdom joined to dove-harmlessness.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines subtil as thin, fine, delicate; nice, acute; sly, artful, cunning, crafty, insinuating.
webster_full: SUBTIL, a. Thin; not dense or gross; as subtil air.
2. Nice; fine; delicate.
3. Acute; piercing; as subtil pain.
4. Sly; artful; cunning; crafty; insinuating; as a subtil person.
scriptures: Gen 3:1
Now the serpent was more subtil than any beast of the field which the LORD God had made. And he said unto the woman, Yea, hath God said, Ye shall not eat of every tree of the garden?
But Amnon had a friend, whose name was Jonadab, the son of Shimeah David's brother: and Jonadab was a very subtil man.
Pro 22:3
A prudent man foreseeth the evil, and hideth himself: but the simple pass on, and are punished.
Behold, I send you forth as sheep in the midst of wolves: be ye therefore wise as serpents, and harmless as doves.
corruption_summary: Modern readers picture temptation as an obvious lure, so the actual method — a reasonable question, a fine adjustment to what God said — passes unrecognized.
corruption_paragraphs: Genesis 3 repays close reading because the serpent never states a falsehood in his opening move. He asks a question that misquotes slightly — hath God said, Ye shall not eat of every tree of the garden? — and the fine weave is in that every. God's prohibition covered one tree; the question implies a God who withholds broadly. Eve is drawn into defending God's generosity, and the ground has already shifted. Subtlety works by adjusting the frame, not by contradicting the text.

The same fineness marks modern doctrinal drift. Denials rarely arrive as denials; they arrive as questions about emphasis, tone, and whether a text can really mean that. Paul's fear for the Corinthians was precisely this — lest by any means, as the serpent beguiled Eve through his subtilty, so your minds should be corrupted from the simplicity that is in Christ. The remedy is not suspicion of every question but a settled knowledge of what God actually said.
roots_summary: Hebrew arum (H6175), shrewd, subtle — morally neutral in Proverbs, sinister in Genesis 3; Greek panourgos (G3835) carries the negative sense.
roots_lines: Hebrew arum (H6175) — subtle, prudent; Genesis 3:1 of the serpent, Proverbs 22:3 of the prudent man who foreseeth the evil.
Hebrew ormah (H6195) — subtilty, prudence; Proverbs 1:4, to give subtilty to the simple.
Greek dolos (G1388) — guile, bait; the New Testament's word for the same craft.
usage: “More subtil than any beast of the field” — the first adjective given the enemy.
“Yea, hath God said?” — the method is a question, not a claim.
“A prudent man foreseeth the evil” — the same shrewdness, rightly used.

etymology: From Old French trichier, to cheat. Treachery is not mere hostility but betrayal — the violation of a trust that was freely given.
biblical_def: Treacherous means faithless to a bond. Malachi uses the word five times in one passage, and the covenant it names is marriage: “the LORD hath been witness between thee and the wife of thy covenant… yet is she thy companion, and the wife of thy covenant… therefore take heed to your spirit, that ye deal not treacherously” (Mal 2:14–16). Jeremiah applies it to the nation as an unfaithful wife — “treacherous Judah” (Jer 3:8) — and Proverbs contrasts it with integrity: the transgressors shall be taken in their own naughtiness (Pro 11:6).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines treacherous as violating allegiance or faith pledged; faithless, perfidious, traitorous.
webster_full: TREACHEROUS, a. Violating allegiance or faith pledged; faithless; traitorous to the state or sovereign.
2. Faithless; perfidious; violating the confidence reposed.
scriptures: Mal 2:14
Yet ye say, Wherefore? Because the LORD hath been witness between thee and the wife of thy youth, against whom thou hast dealt treacherously: yet is she thy companion, and the wife of thy covenant.
Mal 2:16

For the LORD, the God of Israel, saith that he hateth putting away: for one covereth violence with his garment, saith the LORD of hosts: therefore take heed to your spirit, that ye deal not treacherously.
Jer 3:8

And I saw, when for all the causes whereby backsliding Israel committed adultery I had put her away, and given her a bill of divorce; yet her treacherous sister Judah feared not, but went and played the harlot also.
Pro 11:6
The righteousness of the upright shall deliver them: but transgressors shall be taken in their own naughtiness.
corruption_summary: Divorce is discussed in the language of incompatibility and personal growth, while the word God Himself uses for it — treachery — is unspeakable in most pulpits.
corruption_paragraphs: Malachi 2 is the passage the modern church most needs and least preaches, because it refuses the vocabulary of misfortune. The men of Judah were not described as having drifted apart from their wives; they were charged with dealing treacherously against the wife of thy covenant. And the LORD is named as the witness to the vow, which makes the betrayal a matter between the man and God before it is a matter between the man and the woman.

The passage also supplies the reason God gives for hating it, and it is pastoral rather than merely legal: that he might seek a godly seed. Covenant faithfulness in marriage is the soil in which the next generation of believers is grown, which is why treachery there has consequences far past the two adults involved. Take heed to your spirit is the repeated command — the guard is placed on the inner life, long before the paperwork.
roots_summary: Hebrew bagad (H898), to act covertly, to deal treacherously — the verb of covenant betrayal, used of Judah as an unfaithful wife.
roots_lines: Hebrew bagad (H898) — to deal treacherously; Malachi 2:10-16, Jeremiah 3:8, 20, Hosea 5:7.
Hebrew bogedah (H901) — treacherous one; Jeremiah 3:7-10, treacherous Judah.
Greek prodotes (G4273) — betrayer, traitor; Luke 6:16 of Judas, 2 Timothy 3:4 of the last days.
usage: “The LORD hath been witness between thee and the wife of thy covenant” — a third party to every vow.
“Take heed to your spirit, that ye deal not treacherously” — the guard is inward.
“Treacherous Judah” — the nation charged as an unfaithful wife.

etymology: From despite, contempt — from Latin despicere, to look down on. Despite is malice with contempt in it, injury delivered as insult.
biblical_def: Despiteful means insolently malicious. Paul lists it in the catalogue of a mind God has given over: “backbiters, haters of God, despiteful, proud, boasters” (Rom 1:30). Christ's command names the same class as objects of prayer: “pray for them which despitefully use you, and persecute you” (Mat 5:44). Hebrews reserves the sharpest use for apostasy, which has “done despite unto the Spirit of grace” (Heb 10:29) — contempt aimed not at a man but at the Spirit who offered mercy.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines despiteful as full of spite, malicious, malignant, as despiteful enemies.
webster_full: DESPITEFUL, a. Full of spite; malicious; malignant; as despiteful enemies.
scriptures: Rom 1:30
Backbiters, haters of God, despiteful, proud, boasters, inventors of evil things, disobedient to parents,
Mat 5:44
But I say unto you, Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you, and pray for them which despitefully use you, and persecute you;

Of how much sorer punishment, suppose ye, shall he be thought worthy, who hath trodden under foot the Son of God, and hath counted the blood of the covenant, wherewith he was sanctified, an unholy thing, and hath done despite unto the Spirit of grace?
Luk 6:28
Bless them that curse you, and pray for them which despitefully use you.
corruption_summary: Contempt has become a public entertainment, and the church has learned to enjoy it toward opponents while calling the enjoyment discernment.
corruption_paragraphs: Christ's command in Matthew 5:44 is specific about the category: pray for them which despitefully use you. He does not ask disciples to reinterpret the malice as a misunderstanding, nor to pretend the treatment was fair. The malice is granted; the response is prescribed. Prayer for a contemptuous enemy is possible only because the one praying has stopped requiring the enemy to be wrong about everything before he can be wished well.

Hebrews 10:29 shows how far contempt can travel. To have trodden under foot the Son of God, counted the blood of the covenant an unholy thing, and done despite unto the Spirit of grace is the language of apostasy — and the striking thing is which Person is despited. The Spirit is the one who applies mercy, so the sin is contempt precisely at the point where kindness was offered. That is why the passage treats it as the end of the road.
roots_summary: Greek hubristes (G5197), an insolent man; epereazo (G1908), to insult, to use despitefully; enubrizo (G1796), to treat with contempt.
roots_lines: Greek hubristes (G5197) — insolent, despiteful; Romans 1:30, and 1 Timothy 1:13, Paul's own former character.
Greek epereazo (G1908) — to insult, use despitefully; Matthew 5:44, Luke 6:28, 1 Peter 3:16.
Greek enubrizo (G1796) — to insult, do despite to; Hebrews 10:29 of the Spirit of grace.
usage: “Backbiters, haters of God, despiteful, proud” — the company contempt keeps.
“Pray for them which despitefully use you” — the malice granted, the response commanded.
“Done despite unto the Spirit of grace” — contempt aimed where mercy was offered.

pos: n. (one habitually intoxicated; rendering Hebrew sabá, Greek methusos)
etymology: From drunk with the pejorative ending -ard. Scripture distinguishes the act from the settled character; a drunkard is defined by habit.
biblical_def: A drunkard is one given to drink. Paul lists the sin among those that bar the kingdom — “nor thieves, nor covetous, nor drunkards… shall inherit the kingdom of God” (1Co 6:10) — and then adds the sentence that transforms the list: “and such were some of you: but ye are washed” (1Co 6:11). Proverbs supplies the clinical description, ending with the drunkard's own resolution to seek it yet again (Pro 23:29–35). Church discipline is directed at the professing drunkard specifically (1Co 5:11).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a drunkard as one given to an excessive use of strong liquor; a person who habitually or frequently is drunk.
webster_full: DRUNKARD, n. One given to an excessive use of strong liquor; a person who habitually or frequently is drunk.
scriptures: Nor thieves, nor covetous, nor drunkards, nor revilers, nor extortioners, shall inherit the kingdom of God.
And such were some of you: but ye are washed, but ye are sanctified, but ye are justified in the name of the Lord Jesus, and by the Spirit of our God.
Who hath woe? who hath sorrow? who hath contentions? who hath babbling? who hath wounds without cause? who hath redness of eyes?

But now I have written unto you not to keep company, if any man that is called a brother be a fornicator, or covetous, or an idolater, or a railer, or a drunkard, or an extortioner; with such an one no not to eat.
corruption_summary: The church swings between treating addiction as pure disease, which removes repentance, and pure choice, which removes compassion — while Proverbs 23 holds both together without strain.
corruption_paragraphs: Proverbs 23:29-35 is the most clinically accurate description of addiction in ancient literature, and it does not moralize. It observes the symptoms — woe, sorrow, contentions, wounds without cause, redness of eyes — then the perceptual distortion, then the seasickness of the man who lies down in the midst of the sea, and finally the line that names the trap: they have stricken me, and I was not sick… I will seek it yet again. The passage grants the compulsion and still holds the man responsible for the seeking.

1 Corinthians 6:11 is the verse that keeps the doctrine from despair, and it is written in the past tense: and such were some of you: but ye are washed, but ye are sanctified, but ye are justified. Paul does not say drunkards are welcome to remain drunkards, nor that they are beyond hope. He says the Corinthian church was partly built out of them. Any congregation that cannot say such were some of us has either forgotten its own history or is not reaching anyone.
roots_summary: Hebrew sabá (H5433), to drink to excess; Greek methusos (G3183), a drunkard; oinophlugia (G3632), excess of wine, in 1 Peter 4:3.
roots_lines: Greek methusos (G3183) — drunkard; 1 Corinthians 5:11 and 6:10.
Greek methuo (G3184) — to be drunken; Ephesians 5:18, be not drunk with wine, wherein is excess.
Hebrew shikkor (H7910) — drunken; Isaiah 28:1, woe to the crown of pride, to the drunkards of Ephraim.
usage: “Nor drunkards… shall inherit the kingdom of God” — the sin named plainly.
“And such were some of you: but ye are washed” — the past tense that makes a church.
“I will seek it yet again” — Proverbs names the trap from inside.

pos: n. (one who wrings gain from others; rendering Greek harpax)
etymology: From Latin extorquere, to twist out. Extortion is gain twisted out of someone by pressure, position, or fear.
biblical_def: An extortioner takes by force or leverage what is not freely given. The Greek harpax means rapacious — the same root as the ravening wolf. Paul bars the professing extortioner from the Lord's table before he bars the pagan one: “if any man that is called a brother be… covetous… or an extortioner; with such an one no not to eat” (1Co 5:11). The Pharisee in the temple thanks God he is not one (Luk 18:11) while Christ charges the Pharisees with being exactly that inwardly: “within they are full of extortion and excess” (Mat 23:25).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an extortioner as one who practices extortion; the illegal or oppressive taking of money by an officer or by any person under color of right.
webster_full: EXTORTIONER, n. One who practices extortion.
EXTORTION, n. The act of taking from another by force or oppression; the illegal taking of money by an officer, or the taking of more than is due.
scriptures: But now I have written unto you not to keep company, if any man that is called a brother be a fornicator, or covetous, or an idolater, or a railer, or a drunkard, or an extortioner; with such an one no not to eat.
The Pharisee stood and prayed thus with himself, God, I thank thee, that I am not as other men are, extortioners, unjust, adulterers, or even as this publican.
Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye make clean the outside of the cup and of the platter, but within they are full of extortion and excess.
In thee have they taken gifts to shed blood; thou hast taken usury and increase, and thou hast greedily gained of thy neighbours by extortion, and hast forgotten me, saith the Lord GOD.
corruption_summary: Extortion survives as a respectable industry — predatory lending, exploitative contracts, ministry appeals aimed at the desperate — while the word is reserved for criminals.
corruption_paragraphs: Christ's charge in Matthew 23:25 is aimed at men who would never have described themselves this way: ye make clean the outside of the cup and of the platter, but within they are full of extortion and excess. The extortion was not armed robbery; it was religious position converted into financial advantage, devouring widows' houses under a pretence of long prayers. Any ministry whose appeals are calibrated to the fear or grief of vulnerable people is doing the same thing with better production values.

Ezekiel 22:12 files extortion inside a covenant indictment, alongside taking gifts to shed blood and taking usury and increase. The prophet's summary is that thou hast greedily gained of thy neighbours by extortion, and hast forgotten me. The forgetting is the root. Where God is genuinely remembered, a neighbour cannot be treated as a resource to be pressed.
roots_summary: Greek harpax (G727), rapacious, an extortioner — the adjective used of ravening wolves in Matthew 7:15; Hebrew ashaq (H6231), to oppress or defraud.
roots_lines: Greek harpax (G727) — rapacious, extortioner; 1 Corinthians 5:10-11, 6:10, Luke 18:11, and of the wolves in Matthew 7:15.
Greek harpage (G724) — plundering, extortion; Matthew 23:25, Luke 11:39.
Hebrew ashaq (H6231) — to oppress, defraud; Leviticus 19:13, thou shalt not defraud thy neighbour.
usage: “With such an one no not to eat” — the professing extortioner disciplined first.
“Within they are full of extortion and excess” — the clean cup, the rapacious heart.
“Hast greedily gained of thy neighbours… and hast forgotten me” — the root is forgetting God.

pos: n. (one who crushes the weak; rendering Hebrew nagas and ashaq)
etymology: From Latin opprimere, to press down. The word describes weight applied to someone who cannot lift it off.
biblical_def: An oppressor presses down those who cannot resist. Scripture's interest is chiefly in who takes the victim's side: “Leave thy fatherless children, I will preserve them alive; and let thy widows trust in me” (Jer 49:11). The messianic King is described by His treatment of them — “he shall break in pieces the oppressor” (Psa 72:4) — and Proverbs draws the line to God directly: “He that oppresseth the poor reproacheth his Maker” (Pro 14:31). Ecclesiastes notes the loneliness of the crushed: on the side of their oppressors there was power, but they had no comforter (Ecc 4:1).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an oppressor as one who oppresses; one who imposes unjust burdens on others; one who harasses others with unjust laws or unreasonable severity.
webster_full: OPPRESSOR, n. One who oppresses; one who imposes unjust burdens on others; one who harasses others with unjust laws or unreasonable severity.
scriptures: Psa 72:4
He shall judge the poor of the people, he shall save the children of the needy, and shall break in pieces the oppressor.
He that oppresseth the poor reproacheth his Maker: but he that honoureth him hath mercy on the poor.
Ecc 4:1

So I returned, and considered all the oppressions that are done under the sun: and behold the tears of such as were oppressed, and they had no comforter; and on the side of their oppressors there was power; but they had no comforter.
Leave thy fatherless children, I will preserve them alive; and let thy widows trust in me.
corruption_summary: The word has been captured by politics in both directions — weaponized as a label, or dismissed as agitation — while Scripture's plain concern for the crushed goes unpreached by either side.
corruption_paragraphs: Proverbs 14:31 makes the doctrine impossible to keep at the level of policy debate: he that oppresseth the poor reproacheth his Maker: but he that honoureth him hath mercy on the poor. Oppression is treated as an insult aimed past the victim at God, because the victim carries His image. That single move removes the question of whether the poor man deserves help; the image is not conditional on his merit.

Ecclesiastes 4:1 is the most honest verse in Scripture about how oppression actually feels, and it is repeated twice for weight: they had no comforter. Not no advocate, no policy, no remedy — no comforter. Where the church arrives with opinions but no presence, it has answered a question the oppressed were not asking. The Psalm 72 King breaks the oppressor in pieces, and until He does, His people are the comfort He sends ahead.
roots_summary: Hebrew nagas (H5065), to drive or press, used of Egypt's taskmasters; ashaq (H6231), to defraud or oppress; lachats (H3905), to squeeze.
roots_lines: Hebrew nagas (H5065) — to drive, oppress; the taskmasters of Exodus 3:7, and of the Servant, he was oppressed (Isa 53:7).
Hebrew ashaq (H6231) — to oppress, defraud; Proverbs 14:31, 22:16.
Hebrew lachats (H3905) — to press, crush; Exodus 3:9, I have seen the oppression wherewith the Egyptians oppress them.
usage: “He shall break in pieces the oppressor” — the King defined by whose side He takes.
“He that oppresseth the poor reproacheth his Maker” — the insult aimed past the victim.
“They had no comforter” — repeated twice, the loneliness of the crushed.

etymology: From Latin contendere, to strive together. The Greek philoneikos is literally a lover of victory — the quarrelsome man enjoys winning more than being right.
biblical_def: Contentious describes the person who generates strife. Proverbs returns to it repeatedly and domestically: “It is better to dwell in a corner of the housetop, than with a brawling woman in a wide house” (Pro 21:9), and “a continual dropping in a very rainy day and a contentious woman are alike” (Pro 27:15) — while the same book indicts the contentious man just as plainly: “as coals are to burning coals, and wood to fire; so is a contentious man to kindle strife” (Pro 26:21). Paul ends a church dispute by refusing to argue: “if any man seem to be contentious, we have no such custom, neither the churches of God” (1Co 11:16).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines contentious as apt to contend, given to angry debate, quarrelsome, perverse.
webster_full: CONTENTIOUS, a. Apt to contend; given to angry debate; quarrelsome; perverse.
2. Relating to contention in law; relating to litigation.
3. Exciting or adapted to provoke contention.
scriptures: Pro 21:9
It is better to dwell in a corner of the housetop, than with a brawling woman in a wide house.
As coals are to burning coals, and wood to fire; so is a contentious man to kindle strife.
A continual dropping in a very rainy day and a contentious woman are alike.
But if any man seem to be contentious, we have no such custom, neither the churches of God.
corruption_summary: Contentiousness now passes for conviction online, where the reward structure pays for heat, and Christians mistake a taste for combat for a burden for truth.
corruption_paragraphs: Proverbs 26:21 identifies the contentious man by function rather than by opinion: as coals are to burning coals, and wood to fire; so is a contentious man to kindle strife. He is fuel. Wherever he goes, existing warmth becomes fire. This is a diagnosis available by observation and immune to the sufferer's self-assessment, since every contentious person believes each particular fight was necessary. The pattern, not the instance, is the evidence.

Paul's method in 1 Corinthians 11:16 is worth imitating and almost never imitated. Having given his reasoning, he declines to keep arguing: if any man seem to be contentious, we have no such custom, neither the churches of God. He does not concede, escalate, or match the energy. He states the practice of the churches and stops. Some disputes are ended not by winning but by refusing to supply more fuel.
roots_summary: Hebrew midyan (H4066), strife, contention; Greek philoneikos (G5380), fond of strife, literally a lover of victory; eritheia (G2052), factious ambition.
roots_lines: Hebrew midyan (H4066) — contention, strife; Proverbs 21:9, 19, 26:21, 27:15.
Greek philoneikos (G5380) — contentious, loving victory; 1 Corinthians 11:16.
Greek eritheia (G2052) — strife, factiousness; Romans 2:8, Philippians 2:3, let nothing be done through strife.
usage: “Better to dwell in a corner of the housetop” — the domestic cost of strife.
“So is a contentious man to kindle strife” — diagnosed by function, not opinion.
“We have no such custom, neither the churches of God” — Paul declines to supply fuel.

etymology: Literally not ruleable. The Greek anupotaktos means not placed under order — a thing outside the ranks.
biblical_def: Unruly means refusing to be governed. James applies it to the tongue: “the tongue can no man tame; it is an unruly evil, full of deadly poison” (Jas 3:8). Paul makes it a disqualifier in the elder's household — his children must not be “accused of riot or unruly” (Tit 1:6) — and describes the false teachers of Crete as “many unruly and vain talkers and deceivers” (Tit 1:10). To the Thessalonians he assigns the church a duty toward them: “warn them that are unruly, comfort the feebleminded, support the weak” (1Th 5:14).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines unruly as disregarding restraint; licentious; disposed to violate laws; turbulent; ungovernable.
webster_full: UNRULY, a. Disregarding restraint; licentious; disposed to violate laws; turbulent; ungovernable; refractory; as an unruly youth.
2. Accustomed to break over bounds; as an unruly beast.
scriptures: Jas 3:8
But the tongue can no man tame; it is an unruly evil, full of deadly poison.
Tit 1:6
If any be blameless, the husband of one wife, having faithful children not accused of riot or unruly.
Tit 1:10
For there are many unruly and vain talkers and deceivers, specially they of the circumcision:
Now we exhort you, brethren, warn them that are unruly, comfort the feebleminded, support the weak, be patient toward all men.
corruption_summary: Ungovernability is celebrated as authenticity, and a church that will not warn the unruly — because warning feels unkind — abandons the very people the command was given to help.
corruption_paragraphs: 1 Thessalonians 5:14 is a masterclass in pastoral discrimination, because it assigns four different responses to four different conditions: warn them that are unruly, comfort the feebleminded, support the weak, be patient toward all men. The unruly need warning, not comfort; the feebleminded need comfort, not warning. Most pastoral failure is a mismatch — comforting the rebellious and warning the fragile — and the verse implies that telling them apart is part of the work.

James 3:8 keeps anyone from reading the word as being about other people. The tongue can no man tame; it is an unruly evil. The most ungovernable thing in the congregation is in every member's own mouth, and James has already said that whoever can bridle it is a perfect man, able also to bridle the whole body. Before a church warns the unruly among it, it has to reckon with the unruly member each of its people carries.
roots_summary: Greek anupotaktos (G506), not subject to order; ataktos (G813), out of rank — a military metaphor for a soldier out of formation.
roots_lines: Greek anupotaktos (G506) — insubordinate; Titus 1:6, 1:10, 1 Timothy 1:9, Hebrews 2:8.
Greek ataktos (G813) — out of rank, disorderly; 1 Thessalonians 5:14, and the verb in 2 Thessalonians 3:6-11.
Greek akatastatos (G182) — unstable, restless; James 3:8 of the tongue, and 1:8 of the double-minded man.
usage: “It is an unruly evil, full of deadly poison” — the ungovernable thing is in your own mouth.
“Warn them that are unruly, comfort the feebleminded” — four conditions, four responses.
“Many unruly and vain talkers” — the profile of the Cretan false teachers.

etymology: Old English idel, empty, vain. The Greek argos is a contraction of a-ergos, without work — idleness is a vacancy, not a rest.
biblical_def: Idle means empty of useful work. Christ attaches judgment to idle speech: “every idle word that men shall speak, they shall give account thereof in the day of judgment” (Mat 12:36) — the emptiness itself is the charge. The householder finds men standing idle in the marketplace and sends them into the vineyard even at the eleventh hour (Mat 20:6). Paul warns Timothy that idleness in young widows breeds more than inactivity: they “learn to be idle, wandering about from house to house; and not only idle, but tattlers also and busybodies” (1Ti 5:13).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines idle as not employed; unoccupied with business; unemployed; and as useless, vain, ineffectual, of no importance.
webster_full: IDLE, a. Not employed; unoccupied with business; unemployed; applied to persons.
2. Unemployed; vacant; applied to time.
3. Useless; vain; ineffectual.
4. Trifling; vain; of no importance; as idle talk.
scriptures: But I say unto you, That every idle word that men shall speak, they shall give account thereof in the day of judgment.
Mat 20:6
And about the eleventh hour he went out, and found others standing idle, and saith unto them, Why stand ye here all the day idle?
And withal they learn to be idle, wandering about from house to house; and not only idle, but tattlers also and busybodies, speaking things which they ought not.
Slothfulness casteth into a deep sleep; and an idle soul shall suffer hunger.
corruption_summary: Idleness is now impossible to see, because constant activity conceals it — a person can be occupied every waking hour and still be, in the biblical sense, doing nothing.
corruption_paragraphs: 1 Timothy 5:13 traces a progression the church would recognize if it looked: they learn to be idle, wandering about from house to house; and not only idle, but tattlers also and busybodies, speaking things which they ought not. Idleness does not stay empty. A life with no assigned work does not remain neutral; it fills with other people's business, and the tongue supplies the occupation the hands lack. That is why Paul's remedy is not merely rest but employment.

Matthew 12:36 is the verse that unsettles everyone who reads it slowly. Not every wicked word — every idle word. The standard is not malice but emptiness, speech that carried nothing and cost nothing and was therefore assumed to be free. Christ's point is not to make His hearers mute but to show that nothing is unweighed, and that the cure is a good treasure in the heart, out of which the mouth speaks.
roots_summary: Greek argos (G692), inactive, unemployed, barren; Hebrew atsel (H6101), sluggish — the sluggard of Proverbs.
roots_lines: Greek argos (G692) — idle, unproductive; Matthew 12:36, 20:3-6, 1 Timothy 5:13, Titus 1:12.
Hebrew atslah (H6103) — idleness, slothfulness; Proverbs 19:15, 31:27, she eateth not the bread of idleness.
Greek ataktos (G813) — disorderly; 2 Thessalonians 3:11, working not at all, but are busybodies.
usage: “Every idle word… they shall give account thereof” — emptiness is the charge.
“Why stand ye here all the day idle?” — the eleventh-hour call to the vineyard.
“Not only idle, but tattlers also” — idleness never stays empty.

etymology: From naught, nothing — a naughty man is a man of naught, worth nothing. The modern nursery sense has drained a word that once meant morally worthless.
biblical_def: Naughty in the KJV means wicked and worthless, not merely mischievous. “A naughty person, a wicked man, walketh with a froward mouth” (Pro 6:12) opens the portrait of the man God hates, and Jeremiah's basket of bad figs is “very naughty figs… they were so evil” (Jer 24:2). James commands its removal from the heart: “lay apart all filthiness and superfluity of naughtiness, and receive with meekness the engrafted word” (Jas 1:21). Proverbs 17:4 notes that a liar gives ear to a naughty tongue — wickedness finds its audience.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines naughty as bad, wicked, corrupt; and worthless, of no value or account — the older and stronger sense.
webster_full: NAUGHTY, a. Bad; wicked; corrupt.
2. Worthless; of no value or account. Jer. 24.
scriptures: Pro 6:12
A naughty person, a wicked man, walketh with a froward mouth.
Jer 24:2
One basket had very good figs, even like the figs that are first ripe: and the other basket had very naughty figs, which could not be eaten, they were so bad.
Jas 1:21
Wherefore lay apart all filthiness and superfluity of naughtiness, and receive with meekness the engrafted word, which is able to save your souls.
Pro 17:4
A wicked doer giveth heed to false lips; and a liar giveth ear to a naughty tongue.
corruption_summary: The word has collapsed into a term for children's misbehaviour, so a reader meeting it in Proverbs 6 hears something playful where Scripture is describing a man God abhors.
corruption_paragraphs: The semantic collapse is worth naming because it happens to strong words generally. Naughty once meant of naught — morally void, worth nothing. Proverbs 6:12 uses it to introduce seven things the LORD hates, a passage about sowing discord and devising wicked imaginations. When the same word now means a toddler took a biscuit, the verse loses its teeth, and readers unconsciously downgrade the sin because the English has drifted.

James 1:21 shows the pastoral use: lay apart all filthiness and superfluity of naughtiness, and receive with meekness the engrafted word, which is able to save your souls. The image is of removing a garment before putting on another, and the word-order matters — the laying apart precedes the receiving. A heart still wearing its worthlessness cannot receive the engrafted word with meekness; it argues with it.
roots_summary: Hebrew ra (H7451), evil, bad; belial (H1100), worthlessness — the man of Belial is literally a man of no profit; Greek kakia (G2549), malice.
roots_lines: Hebrew belial (H1100) — worthlessness; Proverbs 6:12, a naughty person is adam belial, a man of naught.
Hebrew ra (H7451) — evil, bad; Jeremiah 24:2 of the figs that could not be eaten.
Greek kakia (G2549) — malice, wickedness; James 1:21, the superfluity of naughtiness.
usage: “A naughty person, a wicked man, walketh with a froward mouth” — a man of naught, not a mischievous child.
“Very naughty figs… they were so evil” — worthless beyond eating.
“Lay apart… superfluity of naughtiness” — the garment removed before the word is received.

pos: n. pl. (those who practise evil; rendering Hebrew raa, Greek kakopoios)
etymology: A compound the translators formed to render a Hebrew participle — not those who did an evil once, but those whose practice it is.
biblical_def: Evildoers names those whose settled practice is evil. The Psalms use it constantly as the class the righteous must not envy: “Fret not thyself because of evildoers, neither be thou envious against the workers of iniquity” (Psa 37:1). Peter turns the word around, describing Christians slandered as evildoers who silence the charge by conduct: “whereas they speak against you as evildoers, they may by your good works, which they shall behold, glorify God” (1Pe 2:12). Isaiah pronounces woe on those who call evil good (Isa 5:20).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an evil-doer as one who does evil; one who commits sin, crime, or any moral wrong.
webster_full: EVIL-DOER, n. One who does evil; one who commits sin, crime, or any moral wrong.
scriptures: Psa 37:1
A Psalm of David. Fret not thyself because of evildoers, neither be thou envious against the workers of iniquity.
Having your conversation honest among the Gentiles: that, whereas they speak against you as evildoers, they may by your good works, which they shall behold, glorify God in the day of visitation.
Isa 5:20
Woe unto them that call evil good, and good evil; that put darkness for light, and light for darkness; that put bitter for sweet, and sweet for bitter!
Psa 37:9
For evildoers shall be cut off: but those that wait upon the LORD, they shall inherit the earth.
corruption_summary: Two failures: envying the prosperity of evildoers, which Psalm 37 forbids outright, and answering slander with outrage rather than with the visible good works Peter prescribes.
corruption_paragraphs: Psalm 37 opens by forbidding a feeling, which is unusual and instructive: fret not thyself because of evildoers, neither be thou envious. The psalm assumes the believer's real temptation is not to join them but to resent their success and quietly wish for it. Its answer is temporal — for they shall soon be cut down like the grass — and the whole psalm is an exercise in lengthening the reader's timeline until the arithmetic changes.

1 Peter 2:12 gives the church its strategy under slander, and it is patient rather than defensive. Having your conversation honest among the Gentiles: that, whereas they speak against you as evildoers, they may by your good works, which they shall behold, glorify God in the day of visitation. Peter does not recommend a rebuttal. He recommends a life that outlasts the accusation, on the assumption that observers eventually notice which report matches the evidence.
roots_summary: Hebrew raa (H7489), to do evil, from ra, evil; Greek kakopoios (G2555), an evildoer — the term Roman officials used of criminals.
roots_lines: Hebrew raa (H7489) — to do harm, act wickedly; Psalm 37:1, 9, Isaiah 1:4, a seed of evildoers.
Greek kakopoios (G2555) — evildoer, criminal; 1 Peter 2:12, 14, 3:16, 4:15.
Greek agathopoieo (G15) — to do good; Peter's prescribed opposite, 1 Peter 2:15, 3:17.
usage: “Fret not thyself because of evildoers” — a feeling forbidden, not just an act.
“They speak against you as evildoers” — the church answers with works, not outrage.
“Woe unto them that call evil good” — the inversion Isaiah names.
